betterCitation: Tang Xianzu, The Peony Pavilion, scene 10, The Interrupted Dream (Bridal Du) (trans. Cyril Birch, 1980)
reason:
THE WORDING HOLDS. I fetched the page the verifier cited rather than trusting its summary of it, and en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Peony_Pavilion returns the couplet in exactly the proposed form, in two lines with a lower case open at the head of the second, and credits it to The Peony Pavilion, trans. Cyril Birch, Bloomington and Indianapolis: Indiana University Press, 2002, p. 44. That is Birch's English and not a paraphrase of it: it renders the celebrated opening of the aria to the tune Zao luo pao, yuan lai cha zi yan hong kai bian, si zhe ban dou fu yu duan jing tui yuan, where duan jing tui yuan is the broken well and crumbling wall that Birch compresses into 'dry well crumbling'. The line ends in a full stop, there is no straight double quote and no dash anywhere in quotation, source or note, and the verse keeps its two lines in the translator's lineation with the poem's own capitals at each line head.

THE LOCATOR AND THE SPEAKER HOLD, AND THE VERIFIER GOT THEM FROM ITS OWN KNOWLEDGE, NOT FROM THE PAGE. This is the one place the evidence overstates itself and I checked it independently. The Wikiquote page carries no scene number and names no speaker, so 'scene 10, The Interrupted Dream' and '(Bridal Du)' are inference, not citation. The inference is right. Wikipedia's scene list confirms that the tenth of the fifty-five scenes is Jingmeng (it gives its own English title, A Surprising Dream); The Interrupted Dream is Birch's title for that scene and is the form in which English scholarship cites it, and Bridal Du is Birch's rendering of Du Liniang throughout his translation. The aria is hers, sung on her first walk in the garden, so the speaker parenthesis is owed and is correctly placed after the locator and before the translation parenthesis, in the order rule 5 asks for.

WHAT I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) Translation drift, which is this track's main failure mode. There is no rival English rendering in circulation that this could be a blurred memory of: the other well known versions of the aria read nothing like it, and the proposal matches the Birch text letter for letter where I can reach it. (2) Misattribution. Tang Xianzu is not on the brief's trap list, the play is his, and nothing here is a roving orphan line. (3) Prose-as-verse. Birch sets the arias as verse and the two lines are printed as two lines; the quotation is not a prose sentence chopped up. (4) Scope. First performed and printed in 1598, drama, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. (5) Publishability. Nothing in it needs a warning. (6) Gates. shipped.js on the exact line with 'Tang Xianzu': shipped [], near [], tang xianzu at 0 of 3 for the year, not banned, not on personsAtCap, and he appears nowhere else in the month's verdicts, so no person stands twice. Source line is 118 characters. Tag Drama is the form of the work and the month is thin there.

THE ONE RESIDUAL RISK, WHICH IS WHY I OFFER A BETTER CITATION WITHOUT REFUTING. The evidence claims 'two independent quotations' of Birch at p. 44. They are not independent: the second is a search engine's restatement of the first, so the page number rests on a single tertiary quotation site and nobody has opened the book. The 1980 first edition is 343 pages over fifty-five scenes (Internet Archive, peonypavilionmud0000tang, Indiana University Press, 1980), which puts scene 10 in the low forties only if the nine short opening scenes run under five pages each; that is likely but it is not verified, and the second edition's pagination has not been checked against the first at all. A page number nobody has seen is the kind of confident detail the standard warns about, and it buys nothing here, because scene 10 plus the aria is already a locatable citation under rule 4. The betterCitation drops the page and names 1980, which is the year Birch's translation was published and so is the year rule 4 asks for; the wording is unchanged because the two editions carry the same translation. If the editor would rather keep p. 44, the line still ships honestly, but then the page is the weakest thing on the card.

THEME. August is impermanence, and this is the purest statement of it in the month: beauty at its fullest opening onto ruin. It is elegiac rather than bleak, and it reads at six in the morning as the poets' half of the blurb.
